title: Method Sets, Embedding, and Interface Satisfaction in Go: The Hidden Contract Behind API Boundaries
description: Go's method set rules determine interface satisfaction at compile time, but the operational consequences surface at runtime in ways that break API boundaries across service layers.
linkedin_post:
Method sets in Go seem like a language spec footnote until you're debugging why a type with all the right methods doesn't satisfy an interface—or worse, satisfies it silently while silently copying mutable state across a service boundary.

In large Go backends—distributed systems, SDK layers, AI integration adapters—the rules around pointer receivers, embedding, and interface satisfaction are load-bearing architecture decisions, not language trivia.

The failure modes I see repeatedly in production codebases:

→ Embedding a struct with pointer-receiver methods by value. The outer type satisfies the interface only via a pointer to itself. Any mutation inside the embedded type operates on a copy. Cache misses, stale connections, or silent no-ops under load.

→ Interfaces defined in the producer package, wide enough to require eight-method test doubles where two would suffice. Every new method silently satisfied by a no-op base struct, hiding correctness gaps.

→ Constructors that return value types when the type holds a mutex or channel. go vet catches some of this. Value-returning constructors catch none of it.

→ Generic infrastructure that mixes pointer and value constraints, hitting the "method with pointer receiver on non-pointer type parameter" wall at the worst moment.

The fixes are mechanical and enforced at compile time:
- Pointer receivers everywhere on a mutable type
- Embed by pointer when embedded state must propagate
- Interfaces defined at the consumer, sized to what the consumer calls
- Explicit interface satisfaction checks in your package (var _ Interface = (*Type)(nil))
- noCopy guards on types that must never be copied

These aren't stylistic preferences. They're operational invariants that determine whether your test doubles behave like your production types and whether your API boundaries hold under refactoring.
